THE ASSUMPTION LEDGER

What this model assumes. What it cannot establish.

This is a deliberately small, uncalibrated model of one service team. All starting values, thresholds, distributions and decision rules are experimental choices. No historical data have been fitted. The simulation shows consequences of assumptions; it does not verify them.

Production & dependencies

The team starts with 5,000 human hours per quarter, ten interchangeable workers, and five complementary stages. Starting quarterly revenue is $400,000; wages are $250,000; other overhead is $50,000. Core output scales with the fraction of its total human effort supplied. This is a simplified dependency rule, not a detailed workflow network. New assignments add separate revenue, with no dependency on core tasks. Successful assignments recur every quarter indefinitely unless stopped. Their revenue has no market saturation or customer-budget constraint; this is a deliberately favorable assumption for new work.

AI & adoption

Core task thresholds are 0.18, 0.36, 0.55, 0.73 and 0.91, each with uniform noise of ±0.06. Capability starts at zero and rises linearly. At threshold, adoption requires four quarters of direct labor savings to exceed integration cost ($30,000 × task share). Core adoption removes all human effort for that stage. This task-by-task rule uses wage-equivalent time savings, not guaranteed cash savings, so adoption can be premature.

New work & uncertainty

Arrivals follow a Poisson distribution. Hours are uniform from 100–500. True quarterly benefit = hours × $50 × payoff multiplier × a uniform draw from 0.25–1.75. Initial beliefs have bounded uniform percentage error and converge linearly to true value over the learning delay, even for unstaffed work. This optimistic learning simplification can be challenged. Negative-surplus mature work closes. A $40,000 concurrent trial labor budget permits weak expected-payoff trials; strong expected-payoff assignments can enter freely. Admission does not guarantee staffing or delivery.

AI pursues new work

In protected-new-work mode, new assignments cannot be automated. In pursuit mode, task-specific AI capability starts at zero when an assignment appears, then rises at the selected rate. Adoption thresholds are uniform from 0.15–0.80. Learning feedback adds the selected strength × cumulative human hours / 2,000. Adoption removes 92% of human hours, leaves 8% checking, and costs $3,000 to integrate. Annual direct savings must exceed this cost. Starting new-task capability at zero is a favorable assumption for humans.

Employer & wages

At each review, the employer compares 0–30 roles, core work first and assignments ranked by expected net benefit per human hour. It maximizes estimated quarterly profit after spreading hiring/exit costs over four quarters. Only a strictly better option changes staffing. The full cost is charged immediately to realized profit. Wages stay fixed by default. Optional wage pressure supplies a lower outside wage: max($50,000, $100,000 × (1 − pressure × automated core share)), rounded to $1,000. A cut costs $2,000 per retained role. Workers are assumed to accept; this is not a bargaining or labor-market model. Wage cuts do not automatically reverse.

Demand & boundaries

Half of core direct unit-cost savings, measured at the starting $50 hourly wage, reduces price. Demand = (starting price / new price)elasticity, capped at 3×. Elasticity zero fixes demand. AI unit cost is constant. There is no competition, wage-income spending loop, capital constraint, bankruptcy, worker mobility, or unemployment duration. Role count is capped at 30 and wages are nominal. The model cannot establish economy-wide unemployment or inequality.

What counts as support?

Established-work bricks indicate paid capacity assigned to core or mature work; experimental bricks indicate trial assignments. Neither colour independently establishes that the wage is justified. Viability is tested for the whole team against alternative staffing arrangements, using management’s beliefs. Unassigned capacity can persist between reviews or because changing it costs more than expected savings. “Collapse” means a change to an existing role–wage arrangement, not necessarily permanent unemployment.

How to challenge a result

Start with constant AI to check stability. Compare protected new work with AI pursuit using the same seed. Turn on demand growth, change transition costs, vary new-work payoffs, and repeat across seeds. A sustained wage bill is as legitimate a result as contraction. The displayed percentile ranges cover random draws only; different structural rules may produce different results.

Model v1.0 · Five years / 20 quarters · Currency is USD for the $1,000-brick convention. No empirical calibration or probability forecast.

WAGE TOWERS A model to question, not a conclusion to inherit.
